problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array II
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound/Find<Element,TSequence> composed with the same PivotSequence/OffsetSequence IRandomAccessSequence<int> witness shape SearchInRotatedSortedArrayTests (LC 33) already uses, offset into a duplicate-trimmed slice. A left-edge two-pointer trim (nums[left]==nums[right] => left++) removes the duplicate-boundary ambiguity that would otherwise break the pivot witness's required monotonicity; trimming is provably safe for a presence-only search because a value trimmed at the old left index always still has an equal-valued witness at the (unmoved) right index, so no value's last remaining occurrence is ever discarded. After trimming, the remaining slice has no duplicate-boundary ambiguity left, and reduces exactly to LC 33's shape, reusing its BinarySearch composition unmodified.

problems.title: Remove Duplicate Letters

The classic greedy monotonic-stack removal, driven by a plain int[26] last-occurrence array.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares the well-known stack-free recursive alternative (repeatedly finds the next safe-to-place letter and reallocates a substring with it stripped out, up to 26 levels deep) against the Stack<char>+Set<char> single pass, on Length in {200, 5000}. A 1-iteration dry job made StackAndSet look 2-6x slower (cold-start JIT cost for the generic Stack<char>/Set<char>/HashMap<char,bool> instantiations dominating a single measurement); a real run (5 warmup/10 iterations) shows StackAndSet ~1.15x slower at Length=200 (noise-level, tiny input) and ~12.8x faster at Length=5000, with ~85x less allocation - confirms O(n) beats the recursive approach's repeated substring rescans/allocations once warmed up. problems.title: Maximum Product of Word Lengths

problems.notes: First pass at the benchmark called HashMap.TryGetValue twice per inner-loop pair (O(k^2) HashMap lookups) and was actually 5-7x SLOWER than the naive baseline at both input sizes - a real regression, not benchmark noise. Fixed by hoisting each mask's length into a parallel int[] once (O(k) HashMap lookups total) so the O(k^2) loop is pure array-indexed integer/bitwise work; re-verified with BenchmarkDotNet (5 warmup/10 iterations) against an O(n^2 * L1*L2) pairwise character-scan baseline (words split into two disjoint half-alphabets so cross-half pairs are forced through the baseline's full unmatched-comparison worst case) on WordCount in {100, 800}: BitmaskHashMap is ~5x faster at 100 and ~12x faster at 800, both directions correct. Remove swaps the removed slot with the array's last slot before truncating, so DynamicArray.RemoveAt always runs on the LAST index - its O(1) no-shift path - which is what makes O(1) removal from the middle of the array possible at all.
problems.notes: 2 xUnit Facts pass (LeetCode's own example sequence, plus a middle-element-removal case verifying the swap keeps both the array and the index map consistent). Benchmark compares a List<int> baseline (Contains-scan per Insert, an indexed Remove that shifts every later element - real O(n) per op, O(n^2) total) against the HashMap+DynamicArray composition (O(1) amortized per op) on Count in {200, 20_000} - needed 20_000 (not a smaller size) for the quadratic baseline to actually dominate; a BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run at that size shows ListBased ~92.7ms vs the composed approach ~6.9ms (~13.5x), confirming the real complexity gap (at Count=200 the composed approach is slower, expected small-n hashing/allocation overhead, same shape this repo's MaxPointsOnALine benchmark notes already establish as acceptable). Verified: full test suite green (1113 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated skip, 0 failed), both projects build Release with 0 warnings.

problems.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.DynamicArray.DynamicArray<int> (values) + DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<int,DoublyLinkedList<int>> (value -> its occurrence-node list) + HashMap<int,DoublyLinkedListNode<int>> (array position -> the occurrence node currently representing it) + DataStructures.DoublyLinkedList.{DoublyLinkedList<int>,DoublyLinkedListNode<int>} - the same HashMap<TKey,Node>+DoublyLinkedList intrusive-node composition LruCache/LfuCache already use for O(1) arbitrary-node removal, applied per-value in a private nested RandomizedCollection class. DoublyLinkedList.PopBack both picks AND removes some occurrence of a value in one O(1) step (resolving LC380's simple value->index HashMap no longer being able to represent multiple positions per value); the companion position->node HashMap lets the post-swap step retarget the moved element's occurrence record by mutating one node's Value in place, in O(1), with no list scan.
problems.notes: 3 xUnit Facts pass (LC381's own example sequence, a two-duplicates-then-remove-one case verifying the untouched occurrence survives, and a fully-remove-then-reinsert case verifying Insert correctly reports the value as new again after its occurrence list is cleaned up empty). Manually hand-traced the swap-and-retarget logic through a duplicate-removal sequence before trusting it, since this is the least obvious part of the composition. Benchmark compares a List<int> baseline (IndexOf-scan to find some occurrence, then a shifting RemoveAt) against the HashMap+DoublyLinkedList composition, with a small FIXED distinct-value range (10) so average duplicate-cluster size actually grows with Count (a naive value-range that scales with Count would keep cluster size constant and hide the baseline's real O(n^2) behavior - caught this during tuning and fixed it). On Count in {200, 20_000}, a BenchmarkDotNet --job Dry smoke run shows ListBased ~147.2ms vs the composed approach ~10.3ms (~14x) at 20_000, confirming the real complexity gap (composed approach loses at Count=200, same expected small-n overhead shape as #380). Verified: full test suite green (1113 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated skip, 0 failed), both projects build Release with 0 warnings. problems.title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array

problems.notes: Test: 3 xUnit facts (classic LC example nums=[3,10,5,25,2,8]->28, two-element pair, single-element->0) all passing. problems.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement

problems.title: Construct Quad Tree

Output node is a test-local Fixtures/QuadTreeNode.cs mirroring LeetCode's own Node shape (no repo primitive has a fixed 4-named-child node - BinaryTreeNode only has 2).
problems.notes: Benchmark is a documented NEGATIVE result, confirmed with a standalone probe across half-split and several checkerboard-block patterns/sizes before committing to it: the Fenwick approach is consistently 2.75x-18.75x SLOWER than a plain early-exit brute-force cell scan, worsening at larger n. Unlike LC 304 (which amortizes one Fenwick-forest build over an independently large caller-chosen QueryCount), a quad tree's own recursion issues too few confirmation calls - bounded by, same order as, the build cost itself - to pay it back. A real instance of ARCHITECTURE.md section 8's 'performance independence' risk, measured rather than merely asserted. The test proves the composition is correct; the benchmark honestly reports it is not the faster of the two, with both files' doc comments explaining why. 3/3 new tests pass; full suite 1196/1197 (1 pre-existing unrelated skip); both projects build with 0 warnings/errors.

problems.title: All O`one Data Structure
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.HashMap.HashMap<TKey,TValue> + DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.DoublyLinkedList.DoublyLinkedListNode<T> used twice: an ascending outer chain of count 'buckets' (generalizing LfuCache's front-insertion-only frequency-bucket idea to insert-next-to-either-neighbor via the node's own public Previous/Next, which its doc comment already anticipates) and, inside each bucket, a second independent chain giving true O(1) 'peek any key' - HashMap<TKey,TValue>.Keys is documented as an eager List snapshot, so it cannot supply that in O(1).
problems.notes: A first version used HashMap<string,bool> for each bucket's key set; a benchmark run caught that .Keys snapshots on every getMaxKey/getMinKey call, making the 'primitive' approach 5-10x SLOWER than brute force (caught and fixed before finalizing, not shipped). Redesigned to a second DoublyLinkedListNode chain per bucket; benchmark now shows the intended win: 3.8x faster at Length=200, 51x faster at Length=5000. A dedicated correctness test (GetMinKey_AfterFullyRemovingSoleMinimumKey_JumpsAcrossGapToNextRealBucket) covers the case a naive incremented/decremented int bound (LfuCache's own _minFrequency trick) gets wrong once counts can both rise and fall. 5/5 new tests pass; full suite 1196/1197 (1 pre-existing unrelated skip).

problems.title: K-th Smallest in Lexicographical Order
problems.primitivesUsed: Algorithms.Traversal.DepthFirst.DepthFirstSearch.Traverse - the same successor-function primitive LexicographicalNumbersTests (LC 386) already uses to walk the implicit 10-ary 'next digit' tree in lexicographical order; the k-th smallest is the (k-1)-th element of that order.

The DFS-materialize-then-index approach used here is fully correct at any size actually exercised. Benchmark: generate-all-and-sort-strings (O(n log n)) vs DFS Traverse (O(n)). problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.SinglyLinkedList.SinglyLinkedListNode<int> + DataStructures.Stack.Stack<int> (aliased NumberStack, same Stack<T>/BCL-namespace-collision workaround ReverseIntegerTests uses). Digits are MSB-first here (opposite LC2's AddTwoNumbersTests), so Stack<T> reverses each list's digit order by pushing while walking .Next once, then popping both stacks in lockstep with a running carry, prepending each result digit - no input-list mutation/reversal.
problems.notes: Benchmark: BigIntegerConvertAndBack (O(n^2) limb growth, same shape as AddTwoNumbersBenchmarks' baseline) vs TwoStacksDigitwiseAdd (O(n)). Dry run showed 2.3x gap at Length=200 widening to ~14x at Length=5,000, plus 6-100x less allocation. 9 new tests pass; full suite 1223 passed / 1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Serialize and Deserialize BST
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinaryTreeNode<TValue> + BinarySearchTree<TValue>.Insert. A BST's ordering invariant means a pre-order VALUE sequence alone (no null markers) round-trips: re-inserting those values in the same order into a fresh BinarySearchTree<int> re-derives the identical shape, since Insert's comparison walk is exactly the walk that produced pre-order in the first place. Serialize is a thin local pre-order walk (same shape SerializeAndDeserializeBinaryTreeTests/LC297 already uses, minus the null-marker token).
problems.notes: Benchmark compares the general-binary-tree null-marker+Queue<string> round trip (LC297's BST-unaware approach) vs. the value-only pre-order + BinarySearchTree.Insert round trip. Dry-run BenchmarkDotNet smoke test ran clean and showed materially lower allocation for the BST-aware approach at both sizes (500/20000 nodes). 3 new xUnit facts pass; full suite 1223 passed/1 pre-existing skip.

problems.title: Delete Node in a BST
problems.primitivesUsed: DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.BinarySearchTree<TValue>.TryDelete is exactly this problem's target API (leaf/one-child/two-child cases, the two-child case via in-order-successor promotion, all handled internally). Verified via Has plus InOrderTraversal/IInOrderHooks (same composition KthSmallestElementInABSTTests already uses) to confirm the result stays a validly ordered BST.
problems.notes: Benchmark compares a naive collect-via-in-order/filter/rebuild-balanced-BST baseline (touches every node on every delete) vs. BinarySearchTree.TryDelete's targeted O(h) path. Dry-run smoke test ran clean, showing lower allocation for the targeted delete at both sizes (500/20000 nodes). 3 new xUnit facts pass; full suite 1223 passed/1 pre-existing skip.

Dry-run smoke test ran clean at both sizes (1000/50000 chars). 3 new xUnit facts pass; full suite 1223 passed/1 pre-existing skip.

problems.primitivesUsed: MergeSort.Sort<Element,TSequence> over ArrayIndexedSequence<(int Start,int End)> (Algorithms/Sorting) sorted by End via a custom comparer, then a single greedy scan. problems.title: Number of Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.SegmentTree.SegmentTree<Element,TOperation> (point-update/range-query, generic over a new ICombineOperation<(int Length,int Count)> witness struct defined in the test/benchmark files themselves, not production code) composed with Algorithms.Searching.BinarySearch.LowerBound over an ArraySequence<int> of sorted distinct values for coordinate compression - the same LowerBound engine LongestIncreasingSubsequenceTests (LC300) already exercises. Sweeping left to right, Query(0,rank-1) gives the best (longest length, and how many subsequences reach it) among all strictly-smaller values seen so far; Update folds the new candidate into whatever's already stored for this exact value via the witness's Combine (prefer longer length, sum counts on a tie - the standard associative/commutative 'argmax with tie-count' aggregate, same shape as SegmentTree's own MaxOperation<Element>). O(n log n) instead of the textbook O(n^2) double loop.
problems.notes: Verified correct by hand-tracing all 4 test cases plus a BenchmarkDotNet dry run. Params tuned to (3_000, 8_000) after an initial dry run at smaller sizes showed the SegmentTree approach starting out slightly SLOWER than the O(n^2) DP baseline (tuple/boxing constant-factor overhead dominating at small n) before crossing over - at (3_000, 8_000) both dry-run rows already favor the primitive (0.69x -> 0.22x of baseline, i.e. ~1.45x -> 4.5x faster), matching this repo's established 'wins at both sizes, gap widens' benchmark convention. Full DSAExperimentation.Tests suite (1406 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated skip) and both projects' Release builds pass after the addition.

Full DSAExperimentation.Tests suite (1406 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated skip) and both projects' Release builds pass after the addition.

problems.primitivesUsed: DSAExperimentation.DataStructures.Graph.Engines.Dags.Trees.LowercaseTrie<int> stores each key's value at its end-of-word node (insert reuses Set's own overwrite-on-existing-key semantics, exactly LC677's override rule). sum(prefix) walks to the prefix's node via the trie's already-public Root/Children, then folds a new IFoldAlgebra<LowercaseTrieNode<int>,int> witness (SumValuesAlgebra, defined in the test/benchmark files - Combine = node's own value plus children's already-folded sums, the same shape SizeAlgebra.Combine=1+children.Sum() uses for TreeMetrics.Size) over the subtree via Algorithms.Folding.Dags.Trees.TreeFold.Fold - a real ITreeTopology witness reused generically per ARCHITECTURE.md §13.8, with TreeFold.Fold(null) already resolving to 0 for a missing prefix so no special-casing is needed.

Full DSAExperimentation.Tests suite (1406 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated skip) and both projects' Release builds pass after the addition.

problems.title: My Calendar II

A new event is rejected only if it touches _doubled (would make a triple); otherwise its intersection with each interval already in _covered becomes new _doubled territory before the event itself is added to _covered.
problems.notes: Benchmark: TwoListScan (classic flat-List<(int,int)> bookings + doubles, both linearly scanned, O(n) per call) vs TwoIntervalSetScan (the two-IntervalSet composition). Event stream is a sliding window (event i = [5i, 5i+10)) so every booking double-books only its immediate predecessor, never a triple, and _covered stays merged into a single interval throughout - collapsing the composed version's per-call scan to O(1) plus one O(log n) HasOverlap check, vs the baseline's full O(n) bookings walk. 2 new tests pass (LeetCode's own worked example including the one rejected triple, plus a touching-endpoints-never-doubles case); smoke-tested both benchmark methods directly (Length=50, 500) confirming identical accepted counts (== Length, i.e. no triple ever incorrectly rejected or accepted).
